query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: The structural and chemical stability of near‐equiatomic multi‐element nanoparticles at high service temperatures is governed both by high configurational entropy that creates lattice distortions and suppresses atomic diffusion, and by strong interfacial anchoring provided by defect sites on the support. This dual stabilization mechanism minimizes element segregation and nanoparticle coalescence under catalytic/thermoelectric conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Solid-solution, near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles (e.g., Ru-5 MEA-NPs) either dispersed on high-defect density carbon supports or on inert (smooth) substrates.
generation.intervention: Synthesize identical MEA nanoparticles on two types of substrates: one with engineered dense defect sites (e.g., wrinkled or defect-rich carbon supports) and one with minimal anchoring sites (e.g., smooth inert oxide surfaces).
generation.conditions: Thermal treatment under service-regime temperatures: catalysis at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric operation at 473–1923 K, with exposure times consistent with realistic operation conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A combination of lattice distortions from multi-element mixing (entropy stabilization) and support-induced anchoring via defect sites.
generation.mechanism: High configurational entropy in the nanoparticles induces severe lattice distortion, which elevates diffusion barriers and slows atomic rearrangements. When combined with strong local metal–support interactions—particularly at defect sites on carbon supports—the mobility of metal atoms is further suppressed, preventing elemental segregation or phase coarsening. This mechanism ensures stability even under high thermal loads.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical thermal treatments, nanoparticles anchored to defect-rich supports will exhibit less compositional fluctuation, lower signs of phase segregation, and minimal particle coalescence compared to those on inert supports. Measurements such as STEM-EDS mapping and XRD characterization should reveal a more uniform elemental distribution and constant lattice parameters in the defect-assisted case.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles synthesized on smooth or low-defect-density substrates, where only entropy-driven sluggish diffusion is active, but without the additional support anchoring effect.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to ultra-small (<10 nm) near-equiatomic multi-element systems operating in the stated temperature ranges. It may not hold if particle size increases significantly or if the noble-metal fraction is very high (reducing lattice distortion) or if the support interaction is negligible due to choice of substrate or adhesion conditions.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence from simulations (PMC7069714, sections 'Stability of MEA-NPs') and in situ TEM observations (PMC7733500) confirm entropy-induced sluggish kinetics and support anchoring effects separately, the synergistic stabilization mechanism under combined catalytic/thermoelectric service conditions, particularly where low noble-metal content is desirable, remains to be directly validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of MEA nanoparticles with identical composition and size but deposit one set onto a defect-rich carbon support and the other onto a smooth, inert substrate. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature annealing protocols within the catalytic (773–1173 K) and thermoelectric (473–1923 K) regimes. Use in situ TEM and synchrotron XRD to monitor atomic diffusion, phase segregation, and morphological changes over time.
measurements: Elemental distribution via STEM-EDS mapping before and after annealing
Particle size and agglomeration state via high-resolution TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the enhanced stability (i.e., suppressed elemental segregation and minimal coalescence) observed on defect-rich supports is not significantly different from that on inert substrates under identical conditions, or if both sets show similar degradation, then the dual mechanism involving anchoring is not operative. In that case, stability would be governed solely by intrinsic entropy effects and not by support interactions.

cited_evidence.text: The dispersion stability of the MEA-NPs can be explained by the following two reasons. First, we used high temperatures for the MEA-NP synthesis, and as a result, they naturally have high thermal stability. Second, the defects of the carbon nanofibers help to anchor these MEA-NPs onto the substrate with improved thermal stability. In terms of the observed structural stability, we believe that it originates from the entropy stabilization effect. Thermodynamically, multi-elemental mixing increases the mixing of entropy and favors an alloy structure. Kinetically, the mixing among different elements also leads to increased lattice distortion (table S3 for Ru MEA-NPs) and, therefore, sluggish diffusion, which prevents phase separation and elemental segregation (, ). To further verify the structural stability, we performed MD simulations to calculate the self-diffusion coefficient of the Ru element in Ru-5 MEA and compared it with Ru in a binary Ru-Ni alloy. We found that the Ru atoms in the Ru-Ni alloy diffuse about two orders of magnitude (100×) faster than in Ru-5 MEA (Fig. 4C), indicating that the sluggish diffusion in the MEA-NPs is due to the multi-elemental mixing and the resultan

We also simulated the overall diffusion in the MEA-NP using a hybrid MC + MD simulation approach, in which the MC swaps were attempted at a constant frequency during the MD simulation to model the annealing conditions at 773 K. The entropy-stabilized structure has less atom diffusion due to high diffusion barriers and sluggish kinetics, resulting in uniform elemental distribution after annealing. Figure 4D shows the statistical probability of the nearest composition distributions for each element in Ru-5 MEA-NPs, displaying its microscopic/atomic arrangement of different elements. We found the nearest-neighbor sites of each element equal to its nominal composition with only short-range fluctuations. As a comparison, when it is fully diffusion equilibrated, clear elemental segregation, especially for Ru, Rh, and Ni, is observed (fig. S5A), indicating that the entropy-induced slow kinetics are the key to stabilize the structure for thermal annealing. Similar entropy-stabilization results were also found when there is an extension of MC + MD’s time scale to 50 ns (fig. S5B) and in the Ru-4 MEA-NPs (fig. S5, C and D). cited_evidence.text: The MD simulations indicates that the nanoparticles are quite stable on the edge planes of T-graphite even at extremely high temperatures. To further verify the thermal stability of such nanoparticles, we performed in situ TEM heating on the CNFs decorated with Pt nanoparticles that were synthesized through ex situ Joule heating method. The ex situ formed nanoparticles appear to have very similar morphology to the in situ observations reported in this work. As it can be seen in Fig. 7a, the ultra-fine nanoparticles are located at wrinkled edge planes showing FCC structure (inset of Fig. 7a). The Pt-decorated CNFs are evaluated at various temperatures (573 K, 773 K, 973 K, and 1173 K). As shown in the high angle annular dark field (HAADF)-STEM image in Fig. 7b, the ultra-small Pt nanoparticles are well dispersed on CNF at room temperature (RT). High temperatures are expected to be detrimental to the nanoclusters’ stability, since the nanoparticles would fuse into larger particles to reduce the surface energy at elevated temperatures.
